he.title: קנה לך חבר
he.prompt: חברים יש לקנות, כלומר, לטפח ולהשקיע מאמץ ביצירת הקשרים עמם. משנה זו מופיעה במסכת אבות שייחודית בעיסוקה במידות טובות ודרך ארץ (המאה ה-2, ארץ ישראל).

description.en: The Hebrew Bible includes several stories of friends showing respect and compassion toward one another, like those of David and Jonathan and Ruth and Naomi. It also uses the terms “friend” or “fellow” in the context of commandments such as loving one’s fellow as themselves. Later Jewish texts analyze different types of friendships and how to strive for the ideal friendship, discuss the obligations of friends toward one another, and extol the spiritual benefits of proper friendships.
description.he: בתנ"ך יש כמה סיפורים על חברים המפגינים כבוד וחמלה זה כלפי זה, כמו דוד ויהונתן ורות ונעמי. השימוש במונח "חבר" או "רֵעַ" עולה גם בהקשר הלכתי כמו מצוות "ואהבת לרעך כמוך". מקורות יהדות מאוחרים יותר מפרטים סוגים שונים של חברויות ומכוונים את הדרך לשואפים להגיע לחברות האידיאלית. כמו כן, המקורות דנים במחויבויות של חברים זה כלפי זה, ומשבחים את היתרונות הרוחניים של חברות אמת.

he.title: אהבת הבריות
he.prompt: הלל הזקן קורא ללכת בדרכי אהרן הכהן, שבין השאר הקפיד על אהבת הבריות. המשנה בפרקי אבות מביאה את דבריו של הלל הזקן, שהיה מגדולי חכמי בית שני ונשיא הסנהדרין (המאה ה-2, ארץ ישראל).

description.en: Many biblical characters are described as loving their spouses or children. The Torah commands people to love in specific contexts – like loving one’s fellow, the stranger, and God – and [Song of Songs](https://www.sefaria.org/Song_of_Songs?tab=contents) consists of poetic conversations between two lovers. Jewish texts composed over thousands of years explore the wonders, hardships, and practical manifestations of love.
description.he: דמויות מקראיות רבות מתוארות כאוהבות את בני זוגן או ילדיהן. התורה מצווה על אנשים לאהוב בהקשרים ספציפיים - כמו אהבת הזולת, הגר והאל וגם פרקי מגילת שיר השירים הם למעשה שיח של שירה בין שני אוהבים. מקורות יהדות שנכתבו לאורך הדורות עוסקים בביטויים המעשיים של אהבה וגם בקשיים שבה.

he.title: משה קיבל תורה מסיני
he.prompt: משה רבנו היה הראשון בשרשרת מסירת התורה שניתנה בסיני. מסכת אבות פותחת במשנה שמתארת את העברת המסורה מסיני וכוללת את התורה שבכתב ואת התורה שבעל פה.

description.en: Moses was the greatest prophet in the biblical tradition. Raised by the daughter of Pharaoh in the Egyptian royal family, after he fled Egypt, he married [Tzipporah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/tzipporah1), the daughter of a Midianite priest, [Yitro](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/yitro). After an encounter with God at the burning bush, God sends Moses back to lead the Israelites out of slavery and to [Mount Sinai](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/mount-sinai) to received the Torah and then through the desert to the promised land. Tragically, he is not allowed to enter the land.
description.he: משה היה גדול הנביאים במסורת המקראית. הוא גדל בבית פרעה, ברח ממצרים ונשלח לשם בחזרה על ידי אלוהים כדי להוציא את בני ישראל מעבדות ולהביאם לארץ המובטחת. משה קיבל את התורה בהר סיני כדי למסור אותה לבני ישראל. הוא נפטר לפני כניסת העם לארץ המובטחת.

he.title: הזוגות

description.en: The Torah is Judaism's foundational text, described as given by God to the people of Israel at Mount Sinai. They tell of the origins and development of the Israelite nation and present the foundational laws of Judaism. In some contexts, “Torah” refers broadly to both the Written and Oral Torah, which includes not only the five books of the Torah but the entire Tanakh (Hebrew Bible), rabbinic literature, and any interpretations relating to those texts.

*Avodat Hashem* — ”service of God” in English — is a primary religious objective in many Jewish texts. The first use of the term “service” in relationship to people serving God is in the book of Exodus, describing the expected [worship](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.7.16?lang=he&with=all&lang2=he) of the Israelites upon leaving Egypt. description.en: The struggle to make ends meet and provide for material needs appears from the beginning of the Torah, as figures like Abraham and Sarah confront famine. Later books of the Torah establish a series of commandments designed to support the poor: farmers must [leave](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus.19.9-10?lang=he&aliyot=0) the corners of their fields and gleanings for the needy, debts are [canceled](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.15.2?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=he) every seven years, and the people of Israel are repeatedly commanded to [open their hands](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.15.8?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&aliyot=0) to those in need. en.ai_prompt: Peace, along with justice and truth, is one of the three fundamental bases upon which the world stands. Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel's teaching in Pirkei Avot, a work of ancient rabbinic ethics and wisdom from the land of Israel, emphasizes the essential role of peace in the stability and harmony of the world.

description.en: The Hebrew word for "peace," *shalom,* is related to the Hebrew word that means whole or perfect, *shalem.* This suggests that there is a relationship between peace and wholeness. Judaism values peace very highly, prioritizing it over nearly everything else, as is reflected in biblical, rabbinic, liturgical, ethical, and legal texts.
description.he: שלום הוא ערך מרכזי בתפיסת העולם היהודית ומופיע במגוון הקשרים במקורות היהדות. ברכת השלום חותמת את תפילת העמידה, את תפילת הקדיש והמילה "שלום" היא אחת משמותיו של האל. בספרי היהדות לאורך הדורות השלום נתפס כמצב אידיאלי והרמוני כאשר המחלוקת לגביו היא כיצד ניתן להשיגו, עד כמה נכון לוותר ולהתפשר עבורו וכיצד להכריע כאשר יש קונפליקט בין האמת והשלום.

description.en: Welcoming guests — *hachnasat orchim* in Hebrew — is considered an act of loving-kindness and a commandment in Judaism, described as greater than [greeting the divine presence](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.127a.13?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Modeled most prominently by the biblical character [Abraham](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/abraham?sort=Relevance&tab=notable-sources), welcoming guests can involve housing them, feeding them, and making them feel comfortable.
description.he: הכנסת אורחים היא רכיב חשוב בתוך המצווה הכללית של גמילות חסדים. מלבד פתיחת הבית לאורח, הכנסת אורחים כוללת לינה ומזון, כל זאת מתוך אהבה ובסבר פנים יפות.

questions.question: What does it mean to be deliberate in judgment?

commentaries.summaryText: Sefer HaChinukh emphasizes the importance of taking time in judgment, avoiding hasty decisions, and seeking guidance from those with greater expertise.
It also highlights the crucial role of meticulous investigation in ensuring fair and accurate judgments, emphasizing the need to thoroughly examine witnesses and their testimonies.
Rambam advises judges to delay their verdicts until they have a comprehensive understanding of the case, allowing for the possibility of new information or perspectives to emerge.

questions.question: What is the purpose and nature of 'making a fence around the Torah'?

commentaries.summaryText: Rambam explains that 'making a fence' involves establishing additional safeguards and restrictions to prevent individuals from violating the Torah's commandments, ensuring distance from sin.
Rabbeinu Yonah sees 'making a fence' as an expression of reverence for God, advocating for measures that go beyond the literal requirements of the law to avoid even the possibility of transgression.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Sefer Vayikra, Torah Ohr, Kedoshim 5
commentaries.summaryText: Isaiah HaLevi Horovitz explores the mystical dimension of 'making a fence,' suggesting that it serves as a protection against spiritual impurities and helps maintain sanctity.

questions.question: What is the value of work, and to what extent should one engage in it?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:10:2
commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller believes that work is so crucial for moral behavior that even those who are financially secure should find some form of work to engage in.
Rabbi Yonah Gerondi argues that work is essential for avoiding idleness, which can lead to boredom and even poverty.
Rabbi Bachya ben Asher maintains that while work is important, it should never come at the expense of religious obligations or Torah study.

questions.question: What is the proper relationship between individuals and those in positions of authority?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:10:3
commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller warns against seeking positions of power, as they can be corrupting and lead to negative consequences, even shortening one's life.
Rabbi Yonah Gerondi advises caution when dealing with those in power, as they may only be interested in using others for their own benefit.

questions.question: Who needs to be careful with their words?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:11:1
commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller believes that the mishnah is addressing its words of caution to the sages and not to ordinary people because the words of the sages are heeded by others while no one listens to the commoners.
Rambam argues that everyone should be mindful of their speech, especially in environments where heretical views are prevalent, as words can be easily twisted to support unintended interpretations.

questions.question: What are the consequences of not being careful with your words?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yonah Gerondi warns that careless words can lead to both literal and metaphorical exile, as misinterpretations can spread harmful ideas and distance people from truth.
Bartenura explains that the consequences can be spiritual, with students being led astray by "evil waters" (heresy) and suffering spiritual death due to their misguided beliefs.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Vaetchanan, Torah Ohr 13
commentaries.summaryText: The Shenei Luchot HaBerit draws a parallel to the story of Moses, suggesting that not being careful with words can lead to actual exile and physical hardship.

questions.question: What are "evil waters"?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:11:2
commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller interprets "evil waters" as a metaphor for heresy and distorted interpretations of the Torah, which can poison the minds of those who encounter them.
Avot DeRabbi Natan suggests that "evil waters" can refer to both literal places of hardship and exile, as well as the negative influences and ideas found in such environments.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Shaarei Orah, First Gate, Tenth Sefirah 186
commentaries.summaryText: Shaarei Orah proposes that "evil waters" represent negative spiritual forces that emerge when the flow of divine kindness is disrupted, leading to suffering and hardship in the world.

questions.question: How should one pursue peace?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:12:1
commentaries.summaryText: Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller emphasizes the importance of actively chasing after peace, just like we chase after other important things in life.
Rabbi Yonah believes that true peacemaking goes beyond good intentions; it requires actively seeking out opportunities to make peace in the world.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Bamidbar, Nasso, Beha'alotcha, Derekh Chayim, Beha'alotcha 2
commentaries.summaryText: Shenei Luchot HaBerit highlights the connection between peace and unity, suggesting that Aaron's role as High Priest was ideal because he embodied the interconnectedness of the Jewish people.

questions.question: How should one love others?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:12:2
commentaries.summaryText: Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller reminds us that our love for others should stem from recognizing their inherent value as creations of God, not for any personal gain.
Joshua Kulp suggests that love is a powerful tool for influence and that by showing love to others, we can inspire them to connect with Torah.
Avot DeRabbi Natan encourages universal love and acceptance, urging us to embrace everyone and avoid harboring hatred.

questions.question: How should one bring others closer to Torah?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:12:3
commentaries.summaryText: Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller shares a story about Aaron befriending those who had sinned, demonstrating the power of compassion and connection in guiding people back to the right path.
Avot DeRabbi Natan draws a parallel between bringing people closer to Torah and bringing them under the wings of the Divine Presence, suggesting that our efforts have a profound spiritual impact.

questions.question: What is the meaning of "making one's name great" and what are the consequences of doing so?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:13:1
commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller believes that chasing fame and power will ultimately lead to your downfall, as those things are fleeting and temporary.
Rabbi Yonah Gerondi believes that pride and self-importance cause a person to be forgotten, as true greatness comes from humility and service.
The Derashot HaRan explains that seeking excessive self-importance will inevitably lead to humiliation, as it goes against the natural order of the universe.

questions.question: What is the importance of continuous Torah study and what are the consequences of neglecting it?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbeinu Yonah says that neglecting to continue learning leads to intellectual stagnation and a wasted life, as wisdom is a lifelong pursuit.
Rabbi Joshua Kulp suggests that neglecting Torah study leaves a person's life empty and without purpose, as it provides spiritual fulfillment and guidance.

questions.question: What constitutes proper and improper use of Torah knowledge?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:13:3
commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller further explains that using your knowledge of Torah for personal gain or status is wrong and will have negative consequences, as true knowledge seeks to benefit others.
Rabbi Yonah Gerondi adds that using Torah knowledge for personal benefit ultimately leads to your downfall, as it should be used to serve God and others.
The Maharal teaches that Torah knowledge should be used for the benefit of others and to spread God's wisdom, as true learning is limitless and meant to be shared.

questions.question: What is the primary responsibility of a person in their own self-development?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yonah Gerondi believes that if you don't push yourself to grow, no one else will, so it's crucial to be your own motivator on the path to self-improvement.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Sefer Vayikra, Torah Ohr, Kedoshim 55
commentaries.summaryText: Shenei Luchot HaBerit writes that self-motivation is crucial to self improvement - without it, there's little hope of progress; with it, there's a wealth of divine aid that supports motivated action.
Kalonymus Kalman Shapira, author of Hakhsharat HaAvrekhim, emphasizes the importance of self-awareness to avoid becoming overly self-centered while striving for self-improvement.

questions.question: When is the best time to embark on the journey of self-improvement and spiritual growth?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yonah Gerondi emphasizes the urgency of starting your self-improvement journey now, as every moment is an opportunity for growth that we shouldn't waste.

He also highlights the problem of inertia - the inherent difficultly in starting on a path of improvement.  He offers encouragement to be humble, take feedback to heart, and take steps in improvement.
Rambam suggests that youth is the ideal time to cultivate good habits and positive traits, as it becomes more challenging to change as we age.

questions.question: How should one prioritize Torah study in relation to work and other obligations?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yonah Gerondi believes that prioritizing Torah study above all else leads to greater rewards in the afterlife, even surpassing those who were righteous but didn't prioritize learning.
Ovadiah Bartenura suggests establishing a routine where Torah study takes center stage, with work filling in the gaps when you need a break from learning.
Sha'arei Kedusha advocates for a balanced approach, where both Torah study and work are essential, but the pursuit of wealth should remain secondary to fulfilling your needs and spiritual growth.

questions.question: What does it mean to 'say little and do much,' and how can this principle be applied in our lives?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yonah Gerondi encourages humility and exceeding expectations, advising us to under-promise and over-deliver in our actions, just like Abraham did in the story of the three visitors.
Rambam contrasts the righteous, who let their actions speak louder than words, with the wicked, who make empty promises. He uses Abraham and Efron as examples of each.
Yeshaya M'Yanov highlights the importance of perseverance, showing how the righteous stay committed to their actions despite challenges and the negative whispers of the evil inclination.

questions.question: How should we approach our interactions with others, and what role does a 'pleasant countenance' play in building relationships?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yonah Gerondi emphasizes the power of a happy face, suggesting that showing a cheerful demeanor can uplift others and create a positive environment.
Rambam defines a 'pleasant countenance' as interacting with others calmly and using kind and welcoming words, fostering positive connections.
Avot DeRabbi Natan teaches that a genuine smile can be more valuable than any material gift, highlighting the impact of a warm welcome on building strong relationships.

questions.question: How should one approach doubt in Jewish law and practice?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yonah believes finding a mentor, even someone of similar knowledge, can help navigate uncertainty in Jewish law.
He also emphasizes relying on established principles and thorough understanding rather than estimations or guesswork.
Rambam suggests that having a trusted mentor helps avoid situations that lead to doubt, like estimating tithes.

questions.question: What kinds of speech should we avoid?

commentaries.summaryText: Rambam warns against harmful speech like slander and false testimony, reminding us of the Torah's teachings on ethical communication.
He also cautions against idle chatter and gossip, emphasizing the value of meaningful conversations and the example set by pious individuals who avoided pointless talk.
Rabbi Yonah believes even everyday conversations about business or personal matters should be concise, encouraging us to prioritize silence and avoid unnecessary elaboration.

questions.question: What is the relationship between study and action?

commentaries.summaryText: Bachya ben Asher emphasizes that the true purpose of Torah study is to guide our actions, echoing the teaching that deeds hold greater significance than mere knowledge.
Ovadiah Bartenura highlights the importance of putting learning into practice, suggesting that teaching without action is ultimately meaningless and silence would be preferable.
Yeshaya M'Yanov proposes that silence and contemplation can be even more valuable than study, as they foster a deeper connection with God through introspection and reflection.

questions.question: What are the benefits of silence?

commentaries.summaryText: Rambam explains how silence safeguards us from sin, as excessive talking often leads to transgression and unnecessary risks.
Orchot Tzadikim points out that silence can be a sign of wisdom, as it allows us to appear more intelligent and thoughtful by carefully choosing our words.

questions.question: How do justice, truth, and peace interact and contribute to a stable world?

commentaries.summaryText: The Jerusalem Talmud proposes a chain reaction where justice leads to truth, which in turn fosters peace, emphasizing the interconnectedness of these values in creating a harmonious world.
Rabbi Yonah sees peace as encompassing all positive aspects of the world, highlighting its paramount importance and the numerous benefits it brings.

questions.question: What are the practical implications and applications of justice, truth, and peace in daily life?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yonah emphasizes the responsibility of judges to ensure fairness and truthfulness in their judgments, upholding the principles of justice in practical settings.
He also stresses the importance of individual truthfulness in all aspects of life, urging people to avoid falsehood even in seemingly insignificant matters.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Shemirat HaLashon, Book I, The Gate of Remembering 11:11
commentaries.summaryText: The Chofetz Chaim highlights the importance of peace within households, even suggesting that prioritizing light for the home takes precedence over wine for Kiddush, demonstrating the practical application of peace in daily life.

questions.question: What is the relationship between the giving of the Torah and the creation of the world?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yonah Gerondi believes the world was created with the ultimate purpose of fulfilling the Torah's teachings.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:2:2
commentaries.summaryText: Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller suggests that the world's continued existence hinges on the active study and observance of the Torah's principles.
The Talmud proposes a dramatic idea: the creation of the world was conditional upon the future acceptance of the Torah by the Jewish people.

questions.question: What is the significance of the Temple service?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:2:3
commentaries.summaryText: Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller emphasizes the crucial role of the Temple service in maintaining the world's existence, as taught by ancient scholars.
The Talmud reveals the profound significance of the Temple service as a means of achieving atonement and securing divine favor.
Rabbi Yonah Gerondi explains that after the Temple's destruction, prayer and acts of loving-kindness have taken the place of the Temple service in Jewish life.

questions.question: Is it permissible to serve God with the expectation of receiving a reward?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:3:2
commentaries.summaryText: Tosafot Yom Tov believes serving God out of pure love is the highest form of worship, but serving with the expectation of reward is still permissible and a valid way to connect with the divine.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Vayakhel, Pekudei, Torah Ohr 13
commentaries.summaryText: Isaiah HaLevi Horovitz argues that serving God for reward, whether in this life or the next, undermines the purity of devotion and implies a lack of trust in God's inherent goodness.
Kedushat Levi suggests that expecting reward for serving God can be a stepping stone for beginners on their spiritual journey, eventually leading to a more mature and selfless devotion.

questions.question: What is the role of fear in serving God?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbeinu Yonah believes serving God should involve both love and fear – not fear of punishment, but awe of God's greatness and power.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:3:5
commentaries.summaryText: Tosafot Yom Tov suggests that true fear of God comes from recognizing our own limitations and appreciating the vastness of creation, inspiring a sense of reverence rather than terror.

questions.question: What are the consequences of serving God for the wrong reasons?

commentaries.summaryText: Rambam warns that serving God with ulterior motives can lead to misinterpretations of teachings and the emergence of misguided beliefs.
Mesilat Yesharim explains that serving God for the wrong reasons can hinder spiritual growth and prevent us from attaining true closeness to the divine.

questions.question: Who are the "sages" we should learn from?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:4:2
commentaries.summaryText: Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller explains that the 'sages' referred to in Pirkei Avot are those who have received the oral tradition, passed down from teachers like Shimon the Righteous and Antigonus, all the way back to Mount Sinai.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Maarechet Heidenheim on Pesach Haggadah, Magid, The Four Sons 3:2
commentaries.summaryText: Tevele Bondi suggests that the 'sages' are individuals who are deeply learned in both Torah and ethics, using their knowledge to guide and teach others.
Orchot Tzadikim emphasizes that true sages not only teach Torah but also embody its principles in their own lives, demonstrating the unity of knowledge and action.

questions.question: What does it mean to "sit in the dust of their feet"?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:4:3
commentaries.summaryText: Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller offers a literal interpretation, suggesting that 'sitting in the dust of their feet' refers to the physical act of sitting on the ground near the sages, a common practice in traditional study halls.
Rabbeinu Yonah Gerondi views the phrase as a call for humility and respect towards the sages, emphasizing the importance of honoring their wisdom and guidance.
Rosh suggests that 'sitting in the dust of their feet' means to follow in the footsteps of the sages, emulating their ways and learning from their example to gain wisdom.

questions.question: How should we approach learning from the sages?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:4:4
commentaries.summaryText: Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller compares our attitude towards learning to a thirsty person seeking water, emphasizing the importance of eagerness and enthusiasm in our pursuit of knowledge.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Otzar Midrashim, Midrashim of Rabbi Eliezer, Book of the Ways of Life 6
commentaries.summaryText: Judah David Eisenstein, through Otzar Midrashim, encourages humility and openness when learning from the sages, reminding us not to be overly reliant on our own opinions and to embrace the wisdom they offer.

Rabbeinu Yonah Gerondi, drawing a parallel to a proverb, suggests that we should be receptive and appreciate the wisdom of the sages, even if we don't fully grasp it at first, as their teachings can nourish our understanding over time.

questions.question: What are the practical implications of the teaching 'Let your house be wide open'?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbeinu Yonah suggests that having a 'wide open' house means ensuring there's ample support for those in need within your home.
He also compares this ideal to the hospitality of Abraham, whose home was open on all sides, welcoming travelers from any direction.
Rambam proposes that instead of acquiring slaves, we should prioritize employing the poor and providing them with a place in our households.

questions.question: Why are women singled out in the Mishnah?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Rereading the Rabbis; A Woman's Voice, 1 Sotah 25
commentaries.summaryText: Judith Hauptman suggests that in a society with strict gender separation, even simple conversations with the opposite sex could be seen as inappropriate.
Writing in the 13th century, Rabbeinu Yonah warns that excessive conversation with women can lead to sinful thoughts and distract from Torah study.
Writing in the 12th century, Rambam writes that conversations with women often revolve around matters of sex, potentially leading to negative character traits and an abundance of desire.

questions.question: What are the characteristics of a good teacher?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:6:1
commentaries.summaryText: Tosafot Yom Tov writes that a teacher should generously share their knowledge of Mishnah and Talmud without charging a fee.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Sefer Vayikra, Torah Ohr, Kedoshim 75
commentaries.summaryText: Shenei Luchot HaBerit suggests that a good teacher, like the one advised in Pirkei Avot, nourishes the student's soul by guiding them to a deeper understanding of Torah and facilitating spiritual growth.

Avot DeRabbi Natan emphasizes the importance of a teacher who provides comprehensive knowledge across various Jewish texts, enabling the student to become well-rounded and blessed in their understanding.

questions.question: What is the role of friendship in Jewish life?

commentaries.summaryText: Rambam emphasizes the importance of actively seeking out friends who can help refine one's actions and lead to a better, more fulfilling life.
Rabbi Yonah believes that friends are essential companions for Torah study, offering support, correction, and deeper understanding, ultimately enriching the learning experience.
Derashot HaRan highlights the value of companionship and friendship, suggesting that the mutual support and warmth shared between friends contribute to a more meaningful and fulfilling life.

questions.question: When and how should we judge others favorably?

commentaries.summaryText: Rambam advises judging everyone favorably unless they are known to be wicked, emphasizing the importance of giving people the benefit of the doubt in ambiguous situations.
Rabbi Yonah encourages judging others favorably even when their actions seem questionable, as their intentions might be good or they may have already repented for their mistakes.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:8:3
commentaries.summaryText: Tosafot Yom Tov suggests that even those found guilty should be judged favorably, as they may have erred unintentionally, highlighting the importance of compassion and understanding.

questions.question: How should one define a "bad neighbor" or "wicked person" in the context of Nittai's teaching?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:7:1
commentaries.summaryText: Tosafot Yom Tov differentiates between a "bad neighbor" and a "wicked person," suggesting that proximity and potential for harm are key factors in determining who to avoid.
The Yachin commentary provides specific examples of negative qualities to watch out for in a neighbor, such as anger, arrogance, and jealousy, highlighting the impact on one's spiritual well-being.

questions.question: To what extent should one distance themselves from bad neighbors or wicked people?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:7:1
commentaries.summaryText: Tosafot Yom Tov advocates for both physical and social distance from bad neighbors, even suggesting warning others about their negative influence.
Rambam advises against forming close relationships with wicked individuals to avoid adopting their harmful habits and behaviors.
Rabbi Yonah cautions against even superficial displays of friendship with the wicked, as it can lead to the sin of flattery and insincerity.

questions.question: Is it ever permissible to associate with bad neighbors or wicked people, and if so, under what circumstances?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yonah argues for complete avoidance of the wicked due to the risk of shared punishment and negative spiritual consequences.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:12:3
commentaries.summaryText: Tosafot Yom Tov presents a contrasting perspective, suggesting that limited interaction, such as greetings, can be used to encourage positive change in the wicked person.

questions.question: What are the boundaries of acceptable legal advice or advocacy?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yonah believes that offering legal advice, even if truthful, can create suspicion and bias towards certain judges, similar to how people might favor the advice of a head judge.
Rambam argues that providing legal counsel is akin to manipulating the judicial process, as it involves 'setting up' the judges by influencing their understanding of the case.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:8:1
commentaries.summaryText: Tosafot Yom Tov suggests that offering legal advice, especially to family, is permissible as long as one is not a prominent rabbinic figure who could set a precedent for biased advocacy.

questions.question: How should a judge approach the litigants before and after a judgment is reached?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:8:2
commentaries.summaryText: Tosafot Yom Tov advises that judges should initially view both parties as guilty to ensure a thorough examination of the facts which will lead to the correct ruling.  Once the litigants accept the ruling, they are viewed favorably because accepting a ruling after a quarrel is a righteous act.
Rabbi Yonah believes that after judgment, both parties should be seen as innocent, acknowledging the possibility of error and respecting their acceptance of the court's decision.

questions.question: What is the role and responsibility of a judge within the community?

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot, Pirkei Avot, Introduction 3
commentaries.summaryText: Tosafot Yom Tov emphasizes the heightened ethical responsibility of judges, as their conduct impacts the entire community and sets a standard for behavior.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot, Pirkei Avot, Introduction 3
commentaries.summaryText: He also stresses the importance of judges being accessible to the community and prioritizing justice over personal leisure, ensuring that everyone has access to fair and timely resolutions.

questions.question: Who is the target audience for the advice to be careful with words?

commentaries.summaryText: Ovadiah Seforno believes judges must be cautious with their words to prevent cunning individuals from twisting their statements for personal gain.

commentaries.commentaryRef: Tosafot Yom Tov on Pirkei Avot 1:9:1
commentaries.summaryText: Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller argues that the advice extends beyond judges to anyone involved in legal proceedings who could manipulate information to influence the outcome.

questions.question: What is the primary concern regarding the thorough interrogation of witnesses?

commentaries.summaryText: Rabbi Yonah Gerondi suggests that extensive questioning is crucial to uncover the truth, as inconsistencies and potential lies often emerge through thorough examination.
Avot DeRabbi Natan cautions that excessive questioning could inadvertently provide witnesses with information they could exploit to fabricate or embellish their testimonies.

questions.question: How should one exercise caution with their words during legal proceedings?

commentaries.summaryText: Ovadiah Bartenura advises against speculative statements, as they might inadvertently give litigants or witnesses ideas for constructing false narratives.
Rabbi Yonah Gerondi warns against careless wording during witness examination, as it could reveal weaknesses in the case or provide clues for fabricating testimonies.
